title: Manjushri visits
hook: the bodhisattva of wisdom goes; the room holds countless seats
tomorrow: I'm sick because the world is sick

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Buddha's great disciples refused to visit the sick layman, each one remembering being out-argued. Your line: they all declined. Did you admit someone was right? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-eight.

Finally the Buddha turns to Manjushri, the bodhisattva of wisdom. And Manjushri doesn't pretend it will be easy. Vimalakirti is hard to answer, he says. He sees deep into the teaching, and his speech is quick. But I'll go. The moment he agrees, the whole assembly wants to come along: bodhisattvas, disciples, gods. Two great minds in one sickroom; nobody wants to miss that. So a vast crowd follows Manjushri into the city, toward one small house. Today: Manjushri visits.
screen: `HE IS HARD TO ANSWER.` → `BUT I'LL GO.` → `A VAST CROWD FOLLOWS.`

segments.voice: Vimalakirti sees them coming, and he does something strange. By his power he empties his house. The attendants go, the furniture goes. Nothing is left but the one bed he lies on. Then Manjushri walks in, and Vimalakirti greets him with a riddle. Welcome, Manjushri. You've come without coming, and you appear without being seen. Manjushri answers in kind: so it is. What has already come doesn't come again, and what has gone doesn't go again. The two of them are talking about emptiness before anyone has sat down. And nobody can sit down. That's the next problem, and Shariputra notices it. A little later in the visit he looks around the bare room and wonders where all these people are supposed to sit. Vimalakirti reads his thought and teases him. Did you come here for the teaching, or for a chair? Then he solves it anyway. He asks Manjushri where the finest lion thrones in all the worlds are to be found, and Manjushri names a Buddha in a far-off world. Vimalakirti calls for those thrones, and they arrive, enormous, towering, and they fit into his small room without crowding it. The city outside isn't crowded either. The bodhisattvas grow tall enough to take their seats. The disciples can't climb up until they bow to the Buddha the thrones came from. The sutra calls this kind of thing an inconceivable liberation. A room that held only a bed now holds everyone, and nothing has been squeezed. The house didn't get bigger on the outside. It just made room.
screen: `AN EMPTY ROOM, ONE BED.` · `YOU'VE COME WITHOUT COMING.` · `A TEACHING, OR A CHAIR?` · `LION THRONES IN A SMALL ROOM.` · then, large: `THE ROOM GROWS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: make room for more. Settle, and notice the space you're in: the walls, the ceiling, the air between you and them. Breathe out slowly, and feel the chest make room for the next breath without being asked. Now bring to mind one person, or one feeling, you've been keeping outside. Someone you've been too busy for. A worry you won't look at. Don't fix it. Just let it in and give it a seat, the way that small room held the thrones. See if anything else had to leave. The bell holds the time.
Manjushri visits. The bodhisattva of wisdom goes where the disciples wouldn't, and a bare sickroom holds the whole assembly. Today's word.
Your line: the room grows. Today, when your schedule or your patience feels full, make room for one more person anyway, and see whether anything is crowded. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-eight.

screen: `DAY 1188 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: I'M SICK BECAUSE THE WORLD IS SICK.`

howItsDone: Across Mahayana traditions Manjushri is honored as the bodhisattva of wisdom, shown in images with a sword and a book, and the meeting of Manjushri and Vimalakirti appears in East Asian painting and teaching.

options: empty it, until only your bed is left.
send word that you're too ill for guests.
fork.reveal: he empties the house by his power, then later fills it with lion thrones from another world, and nothing is crowded.

original.note: Sanskrit: Manjushri, the bodhisattva of wisdom, who agrees to visit Vimalakirti.

trapdoor: what you thought: a get-well visit from a famous friend.
what it means: the bodhisattva of wisdom goes where others wouldn't; an empty room holds a whole assembly without crowding.
what a scholar hears: the sutra calls this an inconceivable liberation: the small holds the vast without either changing.
recall: hears it secondhand, and is glad

notes: Paraphrased from the Vimalakirti-nirdesha ch. 5 (Manjushri agrees, the empty room, the greeting) and ch. 6 (Shariputra and the seats, the lion thrones). No translation quoted.
Order: the thrones episode comes after the conversation about illness (tomorrow's day) in the sutra. The script flags this with 'a little later in the visit'; a Keeper may prefer to move it.
Greeting paraphrased ('you've come without coming, and you see without seeing'; Manjushri's reply); confirm the sense.
Thrones: from the Buddha Sumerupradiparaja (or similar) in a world called Merudhvaja; names left out. Confirm that the disciples could sit only after bowing to that Buddha.
'Inconceivable liberation' (acintya-vimoksha) as the sutra's term; confirm.
howItsDone: sword and book iconography and 'a favorite subject in East Asian painting' are reception claims; confirm or cut.
Editor: greeting's second half changed from 'you see without seeing' to 'you appear without being seen', closer to the sense of the sutra's greeting; confirm.
